TODDLER 5 · LESSON 11

Animals and Sounds for 2-Year-Olds

Age 2 YearsSubject Talk & ExploreClass Toddler 5Duration 3–5 minutes

Moo, woof, quack! At two, animal sounds are a game your toddler can already play. This class meets twenty animals — farm friends, wild ones and a few little extras — with big cards, two tap games and sounds to try all day.

There is no reading and nothing to test. You ask, your toddler answers — with the sound, the name, a point or a giggle. Three to five playful minutes is plenty.

Start Class ↓Moo first. Your toddler will join in.

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the animal cards together.

The twelve animal cards live in the flashcards library, each on its own page — with its real sound to hear where a recording is ready — and every page can be printed or drawn on.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Print the animal cards from the flashcards library and cut them out together, naming each animal as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Say the sound

    Hold up one card and make its sound — moo, woof, tweet — then wait. Whatever your toddler sends back is the lesson working.

  3. 03

    Act it out

    Act each animal out with your body: waddle, hop, flap. Toddlers learn the word with the whole body, not just the ears.

  4. 04

    Match card to world

    Keep one card on the fridge and find its twin in a book or out the window. Picture to world, world to picture — that is the whole game.

Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Animals are everywhere.

Spot a bird outside? Listen together. Once you start listening, animals show up all day — no plan needed.

Try one today

  • Pass a dog on the way to the shop? Whisper woof.
  • Moo at breakfast. Quack at bath time.
  • Act out an animal. Can they guess which one?
  • Reading an animal book? Make every sound together.

Keep it playful and stay close by. One animal noticed together is a complete class.

One last word from class.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Sounds come before names. Moo usually arrives before cow — both count as talking.

Add the body: flap like a duck, gallop like a horse, stomp like an elephant. It all counts.

A wrong tap is just a chance to look together. The class never shows a score or a cross.

Age ranges are a guide. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines. Children learn at their own pace.

    Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the animal most toddlers meet first into a two-minute daily game: see the dog, make the woof, find more dogs, and let the word grow out of the sound at its own speed.

    What is this?

    A dog is a furry animal friend with a tail and a big bark — and its sound, woof, is one of the very easiest noises for a two-year-old mouth to try.

    What does it mean?

    Sounds come before names at two: woof often arrives weeks before dog, and that is not a mistake but the normal order. Every woof your toddler attempts is language practice in disguise.

    What does the child need to know?

    The sound is woof — toddlers deliver woof-woof, wuff, or an excited pant, and every version counts. The name often lands as doggie or gog first; the short form comes later on its own.

    Why this matters

    Dogs fill a toddler’s week: walks, parks, books, a neighbour’s garden. That constant replay makes this card the highest-repetition word lesson in the deck, and repetition is the fuel of the vocabulary explosion.

    What it teaches

    Vocabulary growth, sound imitation, and the first link between a picture and a real thing spotted out loud — the seed of all later labelling.

    Words to learn

    dogwoofbarktailpuppywalk

    Say this to your child

    “"Look — a dog! The dog says woof. Can you make the woof? Woof woof! Every dog we meet says woof: dogs in books, dogs out the window, dogs sleeping in the sun."”

    Step by step

    1. Hold the card up and name it twice — dog, dog — then add the sound in the same breath: the dog says woof.
    2. Make the sound together, one woof per clap, so the noise has a beat small hands can join.
    3. Hunt dogs where dogs live: a picture book, the toy basket, the window on walk day. Each found dog earns its woof.
    4. Treat every attempt as an answer — a grunt, a wuff, a point at the card all get a warm "yes, woof!" back.
    5. Return on odd days this week: a breakfast woof, a bath-time woof, until your toddler fetches the card to demand the game.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a dog saying woof, and the sound word sits right there to point at. Ask your child to find the dog, then to find the woof — two finds, one picture.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the dog?" "What does the dog say?" "Can you make the woof sound?" "Can you spot a dog in this book?"

    What your child can say or do

    Expect woof long before dog — a proud "WOOF!" is a complete answer at two. Some toddlers point at the card and wait for you to perform; pointing is an answer too, and an enthusiastic pant counts double.

    Out in the real world

    A real dog on the street is the card come alive. Stop for a second, whisper "woof" together, and the lesson keeps teaching long after the card is back in the drawer.

    Try it together

    Dog walk: crawl across the rug together, woofing at each cushion as if it were a tree. Then swap jobs — your toddler is the dog, you hold the imaginary lead, and the walk ends at the armchair park.

    Understanding check

    Show the card and ask what the dog says. A woof, a wuff or a happy pant all pass. Then open another book to a dog page — if the sound appears there too, the learning has left the card and settled in.

    Parent tips

    Pair sound and name every single time: "dog — woof!" The two words teach each other. If your toddler says gog, echo dog once, warmly, and keep playing; correction can wait for the school years.

    Staying safe

    Real dogs stay behind their owner’s rules: ask the grown-up with the lead before anyone pets, and let your toddler wave and woof from your hip until the answer is yes.

    This lesson pairs with the Dog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Cat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the cat the toddler way: the meow comes first, the creep-and-pounce comes second, and the word cat sneaks in behind both.

    What is this?

    A cat is a soft, whiskery animal that says meow — a sound with two easy parts, mee-ow, that a two-year-old can split and stitch back together.

    What does it mean?

    Meow is a two-syllable sound, which makes it quiet mouth-gymnastics: your toddler is learning to blend syllables long before anyone says the word blending.

    What does the child need to know?

    The meow is a naturally quiet sound, which is why the whisper version belongs in this lesson — dropping your volume keeps the game fresh and teaches that voices have settings.

    Why this matters

    Cats nap on windowsills and fence posts in most neighbourhoods, so the chance to use the word out in the world arrives almost daily. A word used daily is a word kept.

    What it teaches

    Sound imitation with syllable blending, volume control, and gentle-hand practice — the cat rewards soft voices and soft fingers alike.

    Words to learn

    catmeowwhiskerssoftkittenquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"A cat! The cat says meow. Can you say meow? Big meow… and now a whisper meow, like this. Cats creep on their soft feet — can you creep like a cat?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say cat, then meow — the name once, the sound twice.
    2. Meow together at two volumes: a big meow, then a tiny whisper meow behind your hand. Let your toddler pick the volume next.
    3. Creep like a cat across the floor on hands and knees, then "wash" your face with a paw. Your toddler will copy before you finish.
    4. When your child answers with mee, ow, or just a grin and a creep, celebrate it — that is the sound being assembled in public.
    5. Keep the card by the window for the week and meow at any real cat you spot together; one cat a day keeps the word alive.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a cat saying meow. Find the cat together, find the meow word, and ask whether your toddler wants the loud meow or the quiet one today.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the cat?" "What does the cat say?" "Can you do a tiny meow?" "Can you creep like a cat to the door?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Meow!" — sometimes aimed at the dog, which is fine and funny. Your toddler may whisper-meow with a hand over the mouth, or creep one knee forward and look back to check you are watching.

    Out in the real world

    Cats appear on walls, in gardens and at grandma’s house. Each sighting is a repetition: point, whisper "cat — meow", and move on before the cat does.

    Try it together

    Cat and mouse: you squeak and scurry, your toddler cats and creeps. Swap roles after two rounds — being the cat that catches is just as educational as being the mouse that escapes.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the cat says while covering the card. A meow in any volume or dialect passes. Then hand over a soft toy cat — if your toddler pats it gently, the gentle-hands half of the lesson landed too.

    Parent tips

    Whisper-meow is the secret weapon: it reboots a tired game instantly and pulls a wiggly toddler back from the edge of chaos. Keep cat play off the dinner table and the lesson stays welcome everywhere.

    Staying safe

    Only pet real cats when their owner says it is fine, and stroke the back, never the tail. A cat mid-dinner or mid-nap gets waved at, not touched.

    This lesson pairs with the Cat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Cow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the easiest big sound in the deck and stretches it into a whole-body game: a moo from the belly, a cow hunt, and the milk connection named out loud.

    What is this?

    A cow is a big farm animal that says moo — a long, low sound that rumbles, which makes it perfect for toddlers who love to hold a noise.

    What does it mean?

    Moo teaches sustained voicing: holding one sound for three whole seconds is breath control that later helps with singing, blowing out candles and long sentences.

    What does the child need to know?

    Cows live in fields and give us milk — say that link once at breakfast and let it sit. Toddlers file connections away quietly and retrieve them weeks later with no warning.

    Why this matters

    Farm animals are the classic first vocabulary set, and the cow is its anchor. A child who owns moo owns the key that unlocks every farm book on the shelf.

    What it teaches

    Breath control and sustained voicing, first animal categories (farm), and the seed of cause-and-effect talk — the cow makes the milk.

    Words to learn

    cowmoomilkfarmbiggrass

    Say this to your child

    “"Big cow! The cow says moooooo. Can you hold your moo? Hands up like horns — mooooo! Milk comes from cows, so every breakfast gets a little moo."”

    Step by step

    1. Put the card where your toddler sits and say cow, then deliver one enormous moo together.
    2. Add the body: hands curled at the sides like horns, a slow sway, one long moo per sway.
    3. Hunt cows in the room and in books — toy cows, cow spots on pajamas, any black-and-white pattern gets called a cow today.
    4. When your toddler answers with an oo or a whispered moo, moo it straight back bigger; their attempt is the spark, your echo is the applause.
    5. Slip the word into the week: moo at breakfast while the milk pours, moo at a cow in a field through the car window.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a cow saying moo. Find the cow, find the moo, and ask if the cow looks big or little — size words ride along for free.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the cow?" "What does the cow say?" "Can you hold a long, long moo?" "What do we pour on our porridge — where does it come from?"

    What your child can say or do

    A long "moooo" with the whole face involved is the target, but "oo!" or a tiny hum counts as the attempt. Some toddlers will moo at the fridge for a week — that is the lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    Field trips do the heavy lifting: a cow behind a fence, a milk carton in hand, a cow puppet at story time. Name the link between milk and cow once per sighting, no quiz attached.

    Try it together

    Moo choir: everyone in the family moos at a different pitch — high moo, low moo, tiny squeaky moo. Your toddler conducts with a spoon and learns that voices come in sizes.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the cow says with the card hidden. Any moo-shaped noise passes. Then pour milk at breakfast and pause — if a moo arrives unprompted, the connection is built and the lesson is done.

    Parent tips

    Hold your moo longer than feels reasonable — toddlers stretch to match a grown-up’s length, and the stretch is the exercise. Farm books double the mileage of this single card.

    Staying safe

    Watch real cows from over a fence or gate, never inside the field. A cow is many times bigger than a toddler, and even friendly ones do not understand small visitors.

    This lesson pairs with the Cow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Duck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes the duck a full-body event: the quack, the waddle, and the pond visit, with bath time as the daily replay button.

    What is this?

    A duck is a water bird with a flat bill that says quack — a short, punchy sound that lands better the sillier it is said.

    What does it mean?

    Quack packs two consonants into one syllable, a genuine mouth challenge at two. Getting a wacky, wack or even an ah! is progress along a real developmental line.

    What does the child need to know?

    Ducks live on ponds and rivers and paddle more than they fly. Watching real ducks beat any picture: movement, noise and water hold toddler attention like nothing printed can.

    Why this matters

    The duck card pays out all week — pond trips, bath games, the waddle — because it bundles a sound, a walk and a habitat into one small bird.

    What it teaches

    Sound play on a tricky consonant blend, body imitation through the waddle, and early nature knowledge — birds live on water.

    Words to learn

    duckquackwaterpondwaddlebath

    Say this to your child

    “"A duck! The duck says quack quack. Can you quack? Now tuck your wings and waddle — quack, quack, waddle, waddle. Ducks paddle on the water with their flat feet."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card, say duck, then quack quack with a smile — silliness is the method, not a bonus.
    2. Waddle side to side with hands tucked under your arms like wings while you both quack; movement welds the sound in place.
    3. Hunt ducks: the bath, the bookshelf, any yellow toy. Line three yellow things up and quack at each in turn.
    4. When your toddler offers an ack, a quack-ish bark or a waddle without a sound, take it — echo the effort and add one small piece: "quack! You waddled!"
    5. Make bath time duck time for the rest of the week: one quack per splash, and the card propped on the tub edge.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a duck saying quack. Find the duck, find the quack word, then ask whether ducks live in trees or on the water — the card makes the answer findable.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the duck?" "What does the duck say?" "Can you waddle like a duck?" "Where do ducks swim?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Quack!" — or a heartfelt "gack!" — plus a waddle is the full duck experience at two. Some toddlers quack at the bath taps for days; each one is a rehearsal.

    Out in the real world

    A pond trip is the graduation: real ducks, real quacks, real splashing. Stand back a step, quack together, and skip the bread — watching is the whole outing and the ducks stay healthier for it.

    Try it together

    Duck pond in the bath: float a plastic tub-boat, sit the rubber duck aboard, and quack it across the water. Tip it over once for the comedy — ducks resurface, toddlers Howl with joy.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the duck says with the card face down. A quack in any spelling passes. Then watch your toddler’s next bath — if the duck gets a quack without prompting, the card has done its job.

    Parent tips

    The waddle is the retention device: a sound tied to a big silly movement survives the week. If quack stays hard, let waddle carry the game while the consonants ripen on their own.

    Staying safe

    At the pond, hold hands at the water’s edge and stay on the path — toddlers lean towards water the way ducks do. No chasing the birds; watching works better anyway.

    This lesson pairs with the Duck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Sheep — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson pairs the simplest farm sound with the softest idea in the deck: baa, plus wool, plus everything in the house that feels like a sheep.

    What is this?

    A sheep is a woolly farm animal that says baa — a short open sound with an easy b start that most toddlers land on the first try.

    What does it mean?

    Baa and maa arrive together for many toddlers, and mixing them up is normal, not failure. Sorting two similar sounds is sound discrimination, and it sharpens with every hearing.

    What does the child need to know?

    Sheep wear wool, and wool becomes jumpers and blankets. The touch connection — woolly equals sheepy — gives this card a sensory anchor the other farm cards do not have.

    Why this matters

    Baa succeeds fast, and an early win keeps a toddler at the table. Bank the easy sound, then use the wool to stretch the lesson into touch and texture words.

    What it teaches

    Sound discrimination between close pairs (baa/maa), texture vocabulary, and first clothing-chain knowledge — coat to jumper.

    Words to learn

    sheepbaawoolsoftfluffyjumper

    Say this to your child

    “"A sheep! Soft, fluffy sheep. The sheep says baa. Can you say baa? Feel your jumper — woolly and soft, like the sheep’s coat. Baa!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say sheep, then baa — twice, with a woolly voice.
    2. Stroke your own sleeve or a blanket while you baa: the sound travels with the soft feeling.
    3. Send the whole family on a wool hunt — jumpers, hats, teddy, the rug. Every soft find gets a baa.
    4. When your toddler says baa for the goat later this week, smile and model the difference once: "sheep says baa" — then leave it alone.
    5. Baa at the jumper drawer each morning this week; dressing time becomes rehearsal time with zero extra minutes.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a sheep saying baa. Find the sheep, find the baa, and ask what the sheep is wearing — the woolly coat is the detail this card is built on.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the sheep?" "What does the sheep say?" "Can you find something soft and woolly?" "Who is wearing a jumper right now?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Baa!" arrives quickly and gets loaned out to every animal this week — a standard toddler sorting phase, not confusion. Some toddlers will rub their cheek on the card, which is sheep-appropriate.

    Out in the real world

    Woolly socks, teddy bears and granny’s blanket are sheep lessons in disguise. Name the link once per item — "woolly, like a sheep" — and the concept spreads through the whole house.

    Try it together

    Sheep dress-up: drape a soft scarf over your toddler’s shoulders, baa, and shuffle around the room as a flock. Count the sheep as you shuffle — one sheep, two sheep — and numbers sneak in too.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the sheep says. A baa passes instantly. Then hold up two fabrics — if your toddler pats the woolly one when you say sheep, the touch half of the lesson has landed as well.

    Parent tips

    Keep saying sheep correctly even when every animal is baa-ing; the labels sort themselves over weeks. Rotation is the friend here — baa today, baa at bedtime, baa on Thursday, and the sound is permanent.

    Staying safe

    At petting farms, stroke sheep only at the hand-wash station’s rules — animal touches happen by the gate, then everyone washes hands before snacks or thumbs go in mouths.

    This lesson pairs with the Sheep flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Pig — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson lets the pig be ridiculous on purpose: a snuffle along the carpet, an oink with a wiggly nose, and a farm word that sticks because it is funny.

    What is this?

    A pig is a round farm animal with a snout and a curly tail that says oink — a two-beat grunty noise that toddlers find irresistible.

    What does it mean?

    Oink asks for a nasal, scrunchy sound unlike any other in the deck. New mouth shapes are the point: each odd noise stretches your toddler’s sound-making range.

    What does the child need to know?

    Pigs snuffle and root around with their strong noses, which is why the snuffle game belongs to this card. Cartoon pigs and real pigs look different — "pigs come in all shapes" settles it in one line.

    Why this matters

    Funny sounds get repeated, and repeated sounds get learned. The pig is the card a toddler requests again and again, which makes it self-teaching once it lands.

    What it teaches

    Sound variety and imitation, body-part naming (snout, tail), and comedic timing — the first jokes toddlers get are sound jokes.

    Words to learn

    pigoinksnoutsnufflecurlymuddy

    Say this to your child

    “"A pig! The pig says oink oink. Can you oink? Push your nose out like a snout — oink, oink! Pigs love to snuffle in the mud with their strong noses."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say pig, then oink oink with your finger popped on your nose for the snout effect.
    2. Snuffle like a pig: push a soft ball along the rug with your nose, oinking as you go. Hand the ball over and let the snuffling begin.
    3. Hunt pigs in books and toy boxes; spot the curly tail wherever a pig hides.
    4. When your toddler delivers an oyk, a snort or pure giggling, oink back louder — the laugh is the lesson working, not an interruption.
    5. Keep oink on rotation all week: oink at bath time, oink at the muddy puddle on the walk, oink at bedtime once for luck.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a pig saying oink. Find the pig, find the oink, and ask where the pig’s nose is — the snout is this card’s teaching detail.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the pig?" "What does the pig say?" "Can you wiggle your nose?" "Can you snuffle like a pig?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Oink!" with a finger on the nose, or a pure snort which is arguably better. Expect oink to leak into dinner time and the supermarket — pigs travel well.

    Out in the real world

    Muddy puddles are pig habitats: after rain, point and say "a pig would love that puddle." Farms and story books bring real snouts, but the puddle line works on any street.

    Try it together

    Snuffle hunt: hide three small toys in the rug’s folds, then crawl and snuffle them out, nose first, oinking at each discovery. Toddlers who refuse every other game will snuffle.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the pig says with the card out of sight. An oink, a snort or a nose-wiggle all pass. Watch for the nose-touch gesture later in the week — the snout has been filed away.

    Parent tips

    Let the oink be as loud as it wants at home and as quiet as a whisper in public — the loud/quiet switch is a bonus lesson hiding inside the silliness. Muddy-puddle talk earns you extra miles in bad weather.

    Staying safe

    Real pigs are farm animals with strong bodies and no idea how small a toddler is — admire from the fence side, hands flat, at any petting farm.

    This lesson pairs with the Pig flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Horse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes the horse a bouncy ride: the trot, the reins, the giddy-up, with the neigh free to arrive as a trill, a whisper or a full theatrical whinny.

    What is this?

    A horse is a big animal with a long tail and a flowing mane that says neigh — a sound many toddlers make first as a wobbling lip trill.

    What does it mean?

    The lip trill is real progress: your toddler is experimenting with lips and breath the way the neigh actually works. Sound attempts do not have to be accurate to be valuable.

    What does the child need to know?

    A real horse towers over a toddler and moves suddenly, so the honest plan is admiring from a distance first. Over-the-fence viewing is plenty close for a first meeting.

    Why this matters

    The horse card bundles the biggest animal, the bounciest game and a sound that doubles as breath play — high value for one card.

    What it teaches

    Breath and lip control, big-movement imitation through trotting, and size language — bigger than me is the horse’s headline.

    Words to learn

    horseneighmanetrotgiddy-uptail

    Say this to your child

    “"Big horse! The horse says neigh. Can you try? Bounce, bounce — giddy-up! Hold your reins. The horse has a long tail and big hair called a mane."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say horse, then try the neigh — any version, trill included.
    2. Bounce in place on soft knees — a toddler-sized trot — one hand up as a rein, neighing at every bounce. Invite your toddler aboard as the rider.
    3. Hunt horses: rocking horses, hobby horses, horse pages in books — each find earns a bounce.
    4. When the neigh comes out as a raspberry or a giggle, trot it forward: "yes! That is the horse noise!" Attempt beats accuracy at two.
    5. Trot once a day this week — down the hallway, around the kitchen — and neigh from the window when a real horse or a delivery pony goes past.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a horse saying neigh. Find the horse, find the neigh word, then ask where the horse’s big hair is — the mane is named on purpose here.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the horse?" "What does the horse say?" "Can you trot like a horse?" "Is the horse bigger than you or smaller?"

    What your child can say or do

    A lip trill, a neigh-ish whinny or a bouncing "giddy-up!" all count. Many toddlers skip the sound and deliver pure gallop — take the gallop and add the neigh yourself.

    Out in the real world

    Horses appear at paddocks, fairs and riding schools. Watch together from over the fence, name the mane and tail from a safe distance, and let the bigness do the impressing.

    Try it together

    Obstacle trot: cushions become jumps, the rug becomes the meadow, and the hallway is the racetrack. Trot the course together, neighing at each jump — big movement, big sound, nap-friendly tiredness.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the horse says. A neigh, a trill or a bouncing giddy-up passes. Then watch story time — a horse page that triggers a bounce means the card moved in for good.

    Parent tips

    Hand over the reins literally: a scarf or a belt becomes leading-reins, and being the rider gives your toddler control of the game. Big animals stay big in books all week — revisit often.

    Staying safe

    Real horses stay behind fences — hooves move faster than toddler reflexes, and even quiet horses startle. Over-the-fence waving is the whole friendship for now.

    This lesson pairs with the Horse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Chicken — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns breakfast into the classroom: the chicken says cluck, the egg came from a hen, and the whole story gets told while the toast is still warm.

    What is this?

    A chicken is a farm bird that says cluck — a short ticking sound, easy to make, that pairs with the egg story every toddler’s kitchen already tells.

    What does it mean?

    Chicken–egg is a toddler’s first food chain: naming where breakfast comes from plants the seed of all later where-does-it-come-from thinking.

    What does the child need to know?

    Chicken, hen and rooster are three overlapping words; chicken is plenty at two. Keep the other two for later — the deck has a rooster card ready for the fancy version.

    Why this matters

    The cluck is quick to learn, and the egg link gives the word a daily slot at breakfast — a vocabulary word with a built-in reminder every single morning.

    What it teaches

    Everyday-connection thinking, sound imitation, and the first food-story words — egg, hen, breakfast — that later grow into real science talk.

    Words to learn

    chickencluckegghenfarmbreakfast

    Say this to your child

    “"A chicken! The chicken says cluck cluck. Can you cluck? Look — an egg! A hen laid this egg, and now it is our breakfast. Cluck cluck, thank you, hen."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say chicken, then cluck cluck — quick little tick-tock noises.
    2. Peck like a chicken: finger beaks pecking at the palm, one cluck per peck. Your toddler’s hand will copy yours.
    3. At breakfast, hold the egg and tell the chain in your own words: "an egg comes from a hen — this one did, and now it is our breakfast." Then cluck once.
    4. When your toddler answers with a cuck, a kuk or just pecking fingers, peck back and add the word: chicken! Cluck!
    5. Cluck at breakfast every day this week — the egg moment makes the whole game self-restarting.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a chicken saying cluck. Find the chicken, find the cluck, then ask what chickens lay — the egg is the story this card is here to tell.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the chicken?" "What does the chicken say?" "Who laid our breakfast egg?" "Can you peck like a chicken?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Cluck cluck!" or a beaky peck at your palm. Some toddlers will march the egg carton to the fridge announcing cluck — the food chain has taken up residence.

    Out in the real world

    Egg cartons, brunch menus and farm visits all replay this lesson. Carton in hand is the easiest: "eggs live here — a hen made these. Cluck!"

    Try it together

    Egg-and-spoon parade (a boiled egg, a big spoon, a short course across the rug): walk it, wobble it, rescue it. Clucking is mandatory, and the hen gets thanked at the finish line.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the chicken says and who lays eggs. A cluck plus an egg answer passes fully. If your toddler points at toast tomorrow and asks for a hen, take it as a distinction question and enjoy it.

    Parent tips

    Thank the hen out loud at breakfast — gratitude rituals glue vocabulary to routine better than any drill. Keep boiled eggs on hand; the parade is worth the prep.

    Staying safe

    Chicken-play eggs are boiled or plastic, never raw — raw shells splinter and raw egg is not for hands that go near mouths. Wash hands after any real farm contact, before snacks.

    This lesson pairs with the Chicken flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Rooster — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives your toddler the longest sound in the set and permission to fail gloriously: nobody finishes cock-a-doodle-doo, everyone finishes laughing, and both outcomes teach.

    What is this?

    A rooster is the farm’s alarm clock — a proud bird that shouts cock-a-doodle-doo, a five-syllable monster of a sound built for attempting, not perfecting.

    What does it mean?

    Long sounds teach chunking: cock-a-doo-doodle arrives in pieces, and piecing sounds together is the same skill your toddler will later use on long words.

    What does the child need to know?

    Doodle-doo is a perfectly respectable toddler version, and many children settle there for a year. The full version grows on its own; nothing needs fixing.

    Why this matters

    This card is the deck’s comedy summit — and the morning slot is built in, because roosters own sunrise. A sound with a scheduled daily stage repeats itself.

    What it teaches

    Multisyllable chunking, breath support for long sound chains, and the social joy of shared nonsense — family jokes are language glue.

    Words to learn

    roostercock-a-doodle-doomorningloudsunwake

    Say this to your child

    “"The rooster! Cock-a-doodle-doo! Shout it with me — cock-a… doodle… doo! It is a giant sound — well done, what an effort. The rooster shouts it when the sun comes up."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say rooster, then fire the full cock-a-doodle-doo with total commitment.
    2. Try it as a team: you take cock-a-, your toddler takes -doodle-doo, then swap. Teamwork makes the monster manageable.
    3. Hunt roosters in farm books and on toy shelves; every found rooster gets the alarm.
    4. When your toddler’s version collapses into breathless giggles at syllable two, that is success — applaud the collapse and try again.
    5. Give the sound its job: a sleepy doodle-doo when the curtains open each morning this week, until the whole house knows the routine.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a rooster saying cock-a-doodle-doo. Find the rooster, find the sound words, and ask whether the rooster looks proud — the comb-on-top posture is the picture’s joke.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the rooster?" "What does the rooster say?" "Can you say the giant sound?" "Who wakes the farm up in the morning?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Doodle-doo!", "doo-doo-doo!" or an explosive cough of syllables — every attempt is correct. Some toddlers will assign the sound to the sunrise permanently; mornings have been worse.

    Out in the real world

    Farm visits and alarm-clock talk both feed this card. When a real alarm or phone rings, compare: "the rooster is the farm’s alarm — cock-a-doodle-doo!"

    Try it together

    Wake the house: your toddler rooster waits outside the bedroom door, then bursts in with the biggest possible doodle-doo to wake the teddy bears, one bear at a time. Repeat until everyone is awake and nobody minds.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the rooster says. Any multi-syllable attempt passes; two syllables pass too. The real test is spontaneous: tomorrow’s curtain-opening tells you if the sound found its slot.

    Parent tips

    Never smooth this sound into correctness — the struggle is the exercise. Do the duet version at the breakfast table and let your toddler own the loudest syllable; ownership breeds repetition.

    Staying safe

    Farm roosters are loud up close and can flap surprisingly high — hold your toddler at the gate and let the sound carry to you both from a step back.

    This lesson pairs with the Rooster flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Frog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes the frog impossible to teach sitting down: every ribbit comes with a jump, every jump comes with a count, and the pond rules ride along.

    What is this?

    A frog is a small green jumper that says ribbit — a bouncy sound that matches the legs, which is why the two are taught together here.

    What does it mean?

    Sound-plus-movement pairs stick harder than sound alone; the crouch-and-spring gives ribbit a body memory that outlasts the card.

    What does the child need to know?

    A real frog tends to sit perfectly still, which turns one into ideal pointing practice. Real frogs are look-and-leave creatures — hands stay in pockets when the real one appears.

    Why this matters

    The frog converts a language lesson into exercise on rainy days, and the sitting-still real frog teaches watching — a genuinely new skill at two.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor imitation (crouch, spring, land), counting chances with every hop, and the watching-not-touching habit that all nature study reuses.

    Words to learn

    frogribbitjumppondgreenhop

    Say this to your child

    “"A frog! Ribbit! Can you jump like a frog? Crouch down low… and SPRING — ribbit! One more! Frogs sit very still by the pond and then — boing! — they are gone."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say frog, then ribbit — one sound, one little bounce in place.
    2. Crouch like a frog together, hands on the floor, then spring: one ribbit per jump.
    3. Hunt frogs: green toys, frog pages, bath frogs. Line them up and ribbit each in turn.
    4. When your toddler jumps without the sound or ribbits without the jump, supply the missing half yourself and cheer the half they brought.
    5. Set a daily hop count this week — five jumps, five ribbits — and let the number grow only when your toddler asks for more.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a frog saying ribbit. Find the frog, find the ribbit, then ask what the frog is sitting on and where frogs live — the pond is the answer the card points to.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the frog?" "What does the frog say?" "Can you crouch like a frog?" "How many jumps can you do?"

    What your child can say or do

    A standing "ribbit!" followed by a vertical launch is the classic. Some toddlers ribbit every time they hop off a step for a fortnight — each one is a repetition.

    Out in the real world

    Pond edges, garden shady corners and picture books all hold frogs. At a real pond, crouch together, watch, whisper ribbit — and keep hands firmly pocketed.

    Try it together

    Lily-pad league: scatter cushions as lily pads and ribbit-jump from pad to pad across the rug. Missed pads are funny, landed pads get counted, and the whole game is over in four minutes — perfect.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the frog says and what frogs do. A ribbit plus a jump passes completely. Tomorrow’s first sofa dismount, if ribbitted, ends the assessment with full marks.

    Parent tips

    Count the hops out loud every time — numbers ride on movement at this age. Keep the game short; five jumps is genuinely enough, and wanting more tomorrow is the retention plan.

    Staying safe

    Real frogs stay where they sit: look, whisper, hands in pockets. Frog skin is delicate and human hands are far too warm and dry for it — watching is the kind version of loving frogs.

    This lesson pairs with the Frog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Lion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the deck’s loudest sound and teaches it in three sizes: big roar, middle roar, whisper-roar — volume control smuggled into pure fun.

    What is this?

    A lion is the big wild cat with a mane that says ROAR — the sound every toddler already owns from books, songs and the back garden.

    What does it mean?

    Playing with volume teaches that the voice has a dial. Loud and soft are opposite words learned in the body, and opposites are the backbone of early thinking.

    What does the child need to know?

    Roaring can tip into over-excited fast. The built-in answer is whisper lions: the same game at a volume the house can survive, and toddlers find whisper-roars just as funny.

    Why this matters

    The lion is the card a wiggly toddler seeks out on a grey afternoon — it is a permitted explosion, and permitted explosions end naps on time.

    What it teaches

    Volume modulation, emotional release through pretend play, and the mane as a first stand-out feature — spotting details is where observation begins.

    Words to learn

    lionroarloudwhispermanewild

    Say this to your child

    “"A lion! The big cat says ROAR. Can you roar? Giant roar… now a small roar… and the tiniest whisper-roar — shh, the lion is sleeping. Big hair, big voice!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say lion, then ROAR — the biggest roar the living room allows.
    2. Roar in three sizes together: giant, middle, mouse-sized. Hold up hands to show which size comes next.
    3. Hunt lions in books and toy boxes; every found lion gets the size of roar your toddler chooses.
    4. When the roar comes out as a scream, bless it once — then offer the whisper version: "now roar like a tiny lion." The switch resets the game.
    5. Give roars their slots this week: big roar after nap, whisper-roar before bed, and a middle one at bathtime.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a lion saying roar. Find the lion, find the roar word, then ask where the lion’s big hair is — the mane is the detail this card exists to name.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the lion?" "What does the lion say?" "Can you do the giant roar?" "Can you whisper-roar so baby doesn’t wake?"

    What your child can say or do

    A full-body "ROAR!" with the chest pushed out is standard delivery. Whisper-roars arrive with a finger on the lips — that gesture alone is worth the whole lesson.

    Out in the real world

    Lions live in story books, zoo visits and the rug at home. Books are the daily stage: one lion page, one roar, one size chosen by the toddler — the deck’s fastest routine.

    Try it together

    Sleeping lions, toddler edition: everyone roars, then flops down as a sleeping lion, then wakes with one giant ROAR and flops again. It burns the last energy of the day and ends in a lie-down by design.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the lion says. A roar in any size passes. Then ask for the tiny lion — if the volume drops on request, the voice-dial has been installed and the lesson is complete.

    Parent tips

    Own the reset: when roaring tips past fun, go whisper without scolding — the game continues, the volume teaches. Zoo lions mostly sleep, so manage that expectation with one honest sentence before you go.

    Staying safe

    Zoo lions are behind glass and barriers for good reasons — hold your toddler at the rail, and remind them gently that a real roar means the lion is telling everyone this is its home.

    This lesson pairs with the Lion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Elephant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson makes the elephant out of your own arm: trunk up, trumpet on, giant slow stomps — with big versus little riding along for free.

    What is this?

    An elephant is the biggest land animal, with big ears and a long trunk, and it trumpets — a strange, wonderful blast toddlers love to attempt.

    What does it mean?

    Big animal, big steps, big sound: the elephant is where size language gets physical. Bigger, biggest and slow are all taught by the stomp itself.

    What does the child need to know?

    The trumpet sound is genuinely odd — nobody says it right the first time, which is the joke. Pair this card with the mouse card later: biggest and smallest are best learned side by side.

    Why this matters

    One card delivers the week’s biggest movement game and the week’s funniest sound. On a rainy day, the elephant is the entire exercise plan.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor imitation with slow heavy stomps, size vocabulary, and pretend-play with a body part as a prop — the arm becomes a trunk, and imagination flexes.

    Words to learn

    elephanttrunkstompbigearspawoo

    Say this to your child

    “"Elephant! Huge ears and a swooshy trunk. The elephant trumpets — pawoo! Can you swing your trunk? Stomp, stomp, slow and heavy. Nobody is bigger than the elephant!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say elephant, then trumpet — pawoo! — with one arm curved down from your nose: instant trunk.
    2. Stomp slowly around the room together: big animal, big steps, one trumpet per corner.
    3. Hunt elephants in books and toys; fill a basin if you have one, because elephants love water and so does bath night.
    4. When the trumpet comes out as a raspberry or a honk, take it happily and make one yourself — the worse your impression, the more your toddler will correct you, and correcting is thinking.
    5. Stomp once a day this week, and stash the mouse card nearby for the big-little showdown at the end of it.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an elephant trumpeting. Find the elephant, find the trunk, then ask which part swings — the trunk is the feature this card is built to teach.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the elephant?" "What does the elephant do with its trunk?" "Can you stomp like an elephant?" "Who is bigger, you or the elephant?"

    What your child can say or do

    An arm welded to the nose, a pawoo-ish blast, and stomps that shake the floorboards. Some toddlers will water their toys with the arm-trunk — that is pretend play blooming on schedule.

    Out in the real world

    Elephants appear at the zoo, on documentaries and in every animal anthology. Bath time is the daily slot: washcloth trunk, water spray, one triumphant pawoo.

    Try it together

    Elephant water hole: carry scoopfuls of water (or dry pasta) across the room with the arm-trunk curled, and pour them into a bowl. Heavy work, trumpet included, tidies itself up.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the elephant does. A trumpet, an arm-swing or a stomp — any one passes; all three is a parade. Then ask who is the biggest animal they know and listen for the trunk.

    Parent tips

    Let your toddler judge your elephant impression and correct you — being hilariously wrong invites the kind of feedback that builds confident speech. Keep stomps slow; slow stomps are quieter and funnier.

    Staying safe

    Zoo elephants are behind big barriers — admire from the viewing rail. At home, clear the stomp route of toys first: elephant feet and scattered bricks have exactly one outcome.

    This lesson pairs with the Elephant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Monkey — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives your toddler the animal they most wish they were: the climber, the swinger, the ooh-ooh-er — with mirror faces as the practice stage.

    What is this?

    A monkey is a climbing animal with quick hands that says ooh-ooh-ah-ah — the simplest sound in the set and the most fun to perform.

    What does it mean?

    Ooh and ah are pure vowels, the easiest noises a mouth makes, so this card is the confidence win in the deck. Easy wins keep toddlers playing the harder cards.

    What does the child need to know?

    Monkeys do what toddlers dream of: climb everything. The copy-me game channels that — monkey faces in the mirror give the energy a stage without a single piece of furniture scaled.

    Why this matters

    A guaranteed-success sound earns its slot in any bad-mood toolkit. When the day wobbles, the monkey card restarts it in three syllables.

    What it teaches

    Vowel play and facial imitation, expressive performance, and turn-taking in sound games — you go, then I go, which is conversation in embryo.

    Words to learn

    monkeyooh-oohclimbswingsillycopy

    Say this to your child

    “"A monkey! Ooh-ooh-ah-ah — give it a go! Scratch, scratch — beat your chest! Look at my monkey face… now make yours. Monkeys swing and climb all day long."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say monkey, then ooh-ooh-ah-ah with a scratch under each arm.
    2. Beat your chest gently and make your best monkey face — lips out, eyebrows up. Let the mirror in on the game.
    3. Hunt monkeys in books and toy baskets; sock puppets and teddies can be honorary monkeys today.
    4. When your toddler answers with any ooh-shaped noise, ooh back in their rhythm — matching their beat is the strongest yes there is.
    5. Keep the card for daytime play this week and end every session with monkeys going to sleep; the exit ritual saves your bedtime.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a monkey saying ooh-ooh. Find the monkey, find the ooh-ooh, and ask what the monkey is doing with its arms — climbing is the answer this card points at.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the monkey?" "What does the monkey say?" "Can you make a monkey face?" "Can you beat your chest like the monkey?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Ooh-ooh-ah-ah!" delivered at speed, plus a face you never suspected lived in there. Mirror monkeys often turn into twenty seconds of pure performance — applaud the show.

    Out in the real world

    Monkeys live at the zoo, in story books and in every game of copy-me. Playground climbing frames become monkey territory with one sentence: "climb like a monkey — ooh-ooh!"

    Try it together

    Copy-monkey: you make a monkey move, your toddler copies it, then they lead and you copy. Leader-swapping is the whole game, and being copied makes toddlers shine.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the monkey says. Any ooh-ah chain passes instantly. Then check the mirror game — a made-up monkey face on request means imitation has clicked at full strength.

    Parent tips

    End monkey play with the sleep ritual every time — it teaches the ending of games, which is a skill in itself. Keep chest-beats gentle; the gesture is the joke, not the force.

    Staying safe

    Zoo monkeys are quick-fingered grabbers — hold bags, snacks and sunglasses close at the enclosure. At home, monkey climbing stays on the floor cushions, not the bookshelf.

    This lesson pairs with the Monkey flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Owl — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the one card that comes with its own volume: the owl hoots quietly, at night, from a tree — and suddenly bedtime has a soundtrack.

    What is this?

    An owl is a night bird with big eyes that says hoot — a soft, round sound made with rounded lips and a gentle breath.

    What does it mean?

    Owls flip the day: they wake when we sleep. That single fact is a toddler’s first window into different rhythms of life, and hoot gives it a sound to hold.

    What does the child need to know?

    A soft hoot is the wind-down tool of this deck. When evening noise climbs, reach for the owl — hooting is a whispering game, and whispering suits tired toddlers.

    Why this matters

    The hoot earns its keep at the hardest hour of the toddler day. A quiet game that ends in lying down is worth more than any noisy card at 7pm.

    What it teaches

    Gentle breath control, night-and-day concept seeds, and the big eyes as an entry into talking about watching and noticing.

    Words to learn

    owlhootnightquieteyesmoon

    Say this to your child

    “"An owl! The owl says hoot, hoot. Can you hoot? Softly now — owls wake up when we go to sleep. Big eyes watching in the dark. Hoot, hoot. Time to rest."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say owl, then hoot twice — soft and round, lips pushed out.
    2. Dim the lights if it is evening and hoot to each other in the half-dark; the quiet is the game.
    3. Hunt owls in books, on pyjamas, in the toy owl if one exists. Owls wake at night — say that part slowly.
    4. When your toddler’s hoot comes out as a whoop, hoot back softer and wait; owls are patient and so is this lesson.
    5. Make hoot the bedtime guest all week: one hoot as the light goes off, and the card can sit on the shelf till morning.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an owl saying hoot. Find the owl, find the hoot, then ask where the owl’s big eyes are — eyes that watch the dark are the picture’s quiet point.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the owl?" "What does the owl say?" "Can you hoot softly?" "When do owls wake up?"

    What your child can say or do

    A whisper-hoot, a round-mouthed "whoo!" or just big eyes and a finger on the lips. Some toddlers will hoot at the ceiling light all week — the night idea has landed.

    Out in the real world

    Owls live in woods, parks and story books — and in the window at dusk, if you are lucky. A quiet doorstep listen for evening birds is the real-world version of this card.

    Try it together

    Owl hide-and-seek, lying down version: you hoot softly from behind the sofa, your toddler turns their head towards the sound with eyes closed. Ears-only seeking is a calm, new skill.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the owl says. A soft hoot passes best of all. Then watch tonight’s lights-out — one voluntary hoot into the dark means the owl has taken the night shift.

    Parent tips

    Keep this card out of the daytime loud rotation; its power is the quiet. Pair hoot with the last cuddle and the owl becomes a bedtime cue within the week.

    Staying safe

    This is the calm card, so the only safety note is a gentle one: if a real night noise frightens your toddler, name it — "that was a car, not an owl" — and hoot once together to bring the quiet back.

    This lesson pairs with the Owl flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bee — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the buzz and the boundary together: bzzz with your lips, a gentle finger-flight that lands softly, and the one rule said the same calm way every time.

    What is this?

    A bee is a small striped garden visitor that says bzzz — a sound you make with your lips buzzing, which toddlers can do long before they can say bee clearly.

    What does it mean?

    Bzzz is lip-and-breath work: a closed-mouth hum with a wobble. It also carries the set’s first safety idea — exciting things sometimes need watching hands, not grabbing hands.

    What does the child need to know?

    Bees visit flowers and mind their own busy work. The rule this card teaches is short and worth repeating: eyes on the bee, hands by your side. Calm words, the same way each time.

    Why this matters

    The bee card pays twice — a sound every toddler can make instantly, and the first line of the gentle-hands habit that the whole garden year will reuse.

    What it teaches

    Lip-buzzing breath control, gentle-touch practice, and rule learning through repetition — the same words, the same calm voice, until the toddler says them back.

    Words to learn

    beebuzzflowergentlestripeslook

    Say this to your child

    “"A bee! Bzzz! Can you buzz? Lips together — bzzz. Fly your little bee… and settle it softly. Eyes on the bee, hands by our side — bees are busy on the flowers."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say bee, then bzzz with your lips buzzing like a tiny engine.
    2. Fly a finger-bee around the room and settle it softly — onto a flower, a chair arm, your toddler’s knee. The soft landing is the skill being taught.
    3. Hand the flight over: their finger-bee buzzes and lands on your shoulder, the book, the window.
    4. When the finger pokes instead of landing, model the soft landing again without scolding — gentle is practised, not demanded.
    5. Use the same short line at every real bee this week — eyes on, hands still — until your toddler starts saying it for you.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a bee saying buzz. Find the bee, find the bzzz, then ask where the bee is going — the flowers are the destination this card points to.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the bee?" "What does the bee say?" "Can your finger bee land softly?" "What do we do when we see a bee?"

    What your child can say or do

    A lip-buzz that startles them the first time they hear it — bzzz is a sound their own mouth made! Expect the finger-bee to visit your nose often; being landed on is part of the job.

    Out in the real world

    Garden flowers, park borders and window boxes are bee airports. Watch one flower for a minute from a step back — a bee may come, and the rule gets its real rehearsal.

    Try it together

    Flower landing pads: scatter paper flowers on the rug, buzz around, and land on one flower at a time — gently. Buzzing optional, gentle landing mandatory, giggling inevitable.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the bee says and what we do when we see one. A bzzz plus "look, no touch" — in toddler grammar, pointing and pulling their hand back — is the full pass.

    Parent tips

    Consistency is the entire safety method here: identical words, calm voice, every sighting. When your toddler says the rule to you someday, the lesson will have outgrown the card.

    Staying safe

    Bees sting only when squashed or scared, so the rule protects both sides: look, do not touch, and never swat. If a bee lands nearby, freeze together and count to five — it will fly off on its own.

    This lesson pairs with the Bee flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Snake — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the longest out-breath in the deck: a hiss that stretches, a floor wiggle to match, and the one clear rule about real snakes.

    What is this?

    A snake is a long, legless animal with no sound except sssss — more air than voice, which makes it the change of pace after all the roaring cards.

    What does it mean?

    Sustained ssss is mouth-muscle and breath training in one: the same control later needed for blowing bubbles, blowing candles and saying long words clearly.

    What does the child need to know?

    Real snakes are a hands-off animal in every country there is. The card lets your toddler enjoy snakes safely, and the rule gets said the same simple way on every walk.

    Why this matters

    After the loud cards, a hiss resets the room. Parents discover quickly that a long sssss on the walk home is also a remarkably effective quieting spell.

    What it teaches

    Breath extension, tongue-tip control, whole-body wiggling imitation, and first rule-following about live creatures.

    Words to learn

    snakehisslongwiggleslowquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"A snake! Ssssssss. Can you hiss? Long and slow, like air coming out. Wiggle, wiggle — snakes slide on their tummies. Real snakes: we look, we never touch."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say snake, then hiss — sssssss — as long as your breath lasts.
    2. Wiggle together: lie on the floor, arms close, and slither along the rug making the hiss travel with you.
    3. Hunt snakes in books and drawers — belts and ribbons make fine pretend snakes for a careful wiggly parade.
    4. When the hiss comes out as a hissy giggle or a short ss!, stretch yours longer and see if they copy; length grows with practice, not pressure.
    5. Hiss at calm moments this week — the walk home, the bath fill-up — and say the real-snake rule once each time snakes come up.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a snake hissing. Find the snake, find the sssss, then ask what shape the snake makes — long and curly is the answer the card draws.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the snake?" "What does the snake say?" "Can you hiss longer than me?" "Can you wiggle like a snake?"

    What your child can say or do

    A stretched "sssss" with the tongue poking out, or a short hiss and a triumphant floor-flop. Some toddlers hiss at the kettle’s steam — a good moment to add hot, not a snake.

    Out in the real world

    Gardens, zoos and books hold real snakes; ribbons and belts hold the pretend ones. If snakes live near you, the rule travels on every walk — same words, same calm voice.

    Try it together

    Snake parade: hold a ribbon each, wiggle it along the floor to a slow hiss, then coil it up in a circle at the end — snakes rest coiled, and so does the game.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the snake says. An s-shaped hiss passes. Then watch for the wiggle at unexpected moments — a rug-slither during tidying-up means the snake lives here now.

    Parent tips

    Longer hisses come from longer out-breaths, so practise on the floor where bellies can feel the air move. Keep the real-snake rule to one sentence; simplicity is what makes rules stick at two.

    Staying safe

    Real snakes are look-never-touch, always — if you meet one, pick your toddler up, step back together, and save the hiss for the safety of the buggy ride home.

    This lesson pairs with the Snake flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Mouse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson shrinks everything down: tiny squeaks, tiptoe creeping, whisper voices — and the mouse-and-elephant pairing that quietly teaches opposites.

    What is this?

    A mouse is a very small animal with quick feet that says squeak — a tiny high noise that tiny voices are naturally brilliant at.

    What does it mean?

    Squeak is the deck’s smallness lesson: little sound, little animal, little feet. Contrast is how toddlers file concepts — mouse beside elephant teaches both twice as well.

    What does the child need to know?

    Quiet feet find more mice, real and pretend. The tiptoe game is the skill here: slow, controlled walking is a genuine two-year-old achievement dressed as sneaking.

    Why this matters

    The mouse card balances the loud half of the deck and hands you a calm-down game — tiptoe mice are quiet by design, which some afternoons is the entire point.

    What it teaches

    Volume and pitch contrast, controlled slow movement, and the beginning of compare-and-contrast thinking with the elephant as its partner.

    Words to learn

    mousesqueaksmalltiptoequietcheese

    Say this to your child

    “"A mouse! Tiny mouse. Squeak, squeak! Can you squeak? Now tiptoe like a quiet mouse — step, step, step. Look next to the elephant: big, big… and little, little!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say mouse, then squeak — high and tiny, twice.
    2. Creep on tiptoe across the room like quiet mice, and squeak at the exact moment you meet. Small feet, small sound.
    3. Hunt mice in books and drawers; line the mouse card next to the elephant card and ask which one is small.
    4. When the squeak comes out as a shout, shrink it together: "tinier… tinier!" — the shrinking game is the lesson.
    5. Tiptoe once a day this week — to the door, to the bath, to bed — with squeaks saved for the arrival.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a mouse saying squeak. Find the mouse, find the squeak, then put the elephant card alongside and ask which animal is little — the pair is the picture.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the mouse?" "What does the mouse say?" "Can you tiptoe like a mouse?" "Which is smaller, the mouse or the elephant?"

    What your child can say or do

    A pinched "squeak!" or a whispered eek, plus tiptoe steps with arms held out for balance. Expect mice to visit the kitchen regularly — small squeaks in big rooms are the joke.

    Out in the real world

    Mice mostly hide, so books and toys carry this card — but squeak works on anything small: a sparrow, a pebble, a raisin. Smallness is the transferable idea.

    Try it together

    Mouse house: drape a blanket over two chairs, tiptoe in with squeaks, and share one pretend crumb. Squeak, nibble, tiptoe out. Repeat until the house gets too popular.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the mouse says. A tiny squeak passes. Then line up two animal cards — if small gets picked when you say mouse, the contrast has been filed and the lesson is done.

    Parent tips

    Play the elephant-mouse duet at least once: the elephant gets the giant voice, the mouse gets the squeak. Opposites learned in the voice land deeper than opposites explained in words.

    Staying safe

    No real-mouse contact needed — wild mice carry mess and disease, and the pretend version is the whole fun. If a real mouse ever appears, it is a look-from-your-arms event, like all wildlife.

    This lesson pairs with the Mouse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Donkey — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hands your toddler the deck’s comedy crown: hee-haw, sung slowly, sung fast, sung gloomy — a one-sound song that teaches how words are built from bits.

    What is this?

    A donkey is a long-eared farm animal that says hee-haw — a two-part bray that starts high and ends low, which is why it sounds so gloriously wrong.

    What does it mean?

    Hee-haw is high-low in one breath: your toddler is singing an interval without knowing it. Two-part sounds teach that noises have shape, the seed of all later speech melody.

    What does the child need to know?

    Deliver it slow and gloomy at least once — the droopy version is reliably the one that lands the laugh. Nobody is more delighted by the silliness than the toddler.

    Why this matters

    One sound, many performances: hee-haw teaches a toddler that a noise can be stretched, shuffled and staged — the discovery that words are built from parts.

    What it teaches

    Pitch play from high to low, song-building with a single syllable pair, and comic timing — the first jokes toddlers tell are sound jokes they control.

    Words to learn

    donkeyhee-hawfunnylongearssong

    Say this to your child

    “"A donkey! Hee-haw! Can you say it? Hee — haw! Now slowly… heeeee… haaaaaw. The donkey owns the silliest noise on the whole farm, and very, very long ears."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say donkey, then hee-haw — high on hee, low on haw, with the long ears drooping.
    2. Sing it three ways together: fast hee-haw, slow hee-haw, and the gloomy one that ends in a sigh.
    3. Invent a hee-haw song where every verse finishes with the bray — any farm tune you half-remember will carry it.
    4. When your toddler invents a new way to say it — extra haws, double hees — adopt their version immediately; their composition is the milestone.
    5. Assign hee-haw its jobs this week: it opens the toy box, it greets the bath, it finishes the bedtime book.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a donkey saying hee-haw. Find the donkey, find the hee-haw, then ask where the donkey’s ears are — long ears are this card’s best detail.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the donkey?" "What does the donkey say?" "Can you say it slow and gloomy?" "Can you make up a hee-haw song?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Hee-HAW!" with a droopy face, or a haw that arrives without the hee — take it. Some toddlers will hee-haw every animal for a day; the donkey’s fame is brief and glorious.

    Out in the real world

    Donkeys appear at farms, on the beach in some towns, and in every nursery-song book. The beach or paddock version gets the loudest toddler hee-haw on record.

    Try it together

    Hee-haw choir: every family member picks a different hee-haw speed and you sing them in order — fast, slow, gloomy, sleepy. Your toddler conducts and chooses which comes next.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the donkey says. Any hee, haw or haw-hee passes. The real test is the invented variation — a hee-hee-haw or a sung-gloomy haw means sound play has gone creative.

    Parent tips

    Match their tempo once, then offer one alternative — fast after slow, quiet after loud. The contrast is what keeps a one-sound game alive past the third day.

    Staying safe

    Farm donkeys look soft and are stronger than they act — feed nothing, stroke nothing without the farmer’s yes, and keep fingers away from those long, curious lips.

    This lesson pairs with the Donkey flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Goat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the deck’s most confusing sound pair — goat and sheep both say something like maa — and turns the mix-up into the game.

    What is this?

    A goat is a farm animal with little horns and a beard that says maa — a sound that sits between the sheep’s baa and a proper toddler yell.

    What does it mean?

    Telling baa from maa is real sound discrimination: two close noises, two different animals. Sorting close pairs is ear-training that phonics will reuse for years.

    What does the child need to know?

    Goats eat nearly everything and usually answer when you call — a reply that lands like a conversation, and turns a farm fence into the best show in town. Petting zoos have the hand-washing rule for a reason.

    Why this matters

    The goat card sharpens listening at the exact moment a toddler needs it, and it gives farm visits a main event: the animal that talks back.

    What it teaches

    Fine sound discrimination between baa and maa, feature-spotting (the beard), and hygiene habits that stick from the first farm trip onward.

    Words to learn

    goatmaabeardhornsfarmwash

    Say this to your child

    “"A goat! The goat says maa! Can you say maa? Look — a little beard under its chin, and horns on top. The goat answers when you call: maa!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say goat, then maa — with a slight yell in it, unlike the sheep’s soft baa.
    2. Put the sheep card next to it: baa for sheep, maa for goat, and let your toddler point to the right card each time you make a sound.
    3. Hunt goats in books and toy boxes; find the beard every time — it is the goat’s badge.
    4. When baa and maa get swapped, smile and model once — "goat says maa!" — then let the game continue; the ears will sort it within the week.
    5. Save a farm or petting-zoo trip if you can: call maa at the fence, wait, and enjoy the reply. Wash hands straight after.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a goat saying baa in the set’s alt text, but the picture’s beard and horns are the details to find. Ask where the beard is and what sits on top of the head.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the goat?" "What does the goat say?" "Can you find the goat’s beard?" "Who says baa, and who says maa?"

    What your child can say or do

    "MAA!" with attitude, aimed at the sheep card half the time. At the fence, a toddler maa that gets a real maa back is the sound of a lifelong animal-lover being born.

    Out in the real world

    Petting farms and city farms keep goats at kid height behind fences — the perfect setup. Call maa, get the answer, then head straight for the hand-wash.

    Try it together

    Baa-or-maa: you make one of the two sounds, your toddler slaps the right card. Start slow, speed up, and let them call the sounds for you to answer — being the caller is the reward.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the goat says and where its beard is. A maa plus a chin-point passes fully. Mixed-up baas this week are fine — the discrimination arrives on its own schedule.

    Parent tips

    The pointing version of this game matters more than the saying: toddlers can show they hear a difference before their mouths can make one. Hands get washed at every farm, no exceptions, no negotiation.

    Staying safe

    Goats nibble fingers, sleeves and anything dangling — keep hands flat and snacks zipped away. Every animal touch at a petting zoo ends at the sink, before anything goes near a mouth.

    This lesson pairs with the Goat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bird — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the deck’s everyday animal into an ears-open habit: listen, point, whisper "bird!" — a game with no table, no props and no end.

    What is this?

    A bird is a flying animal with wings that says tweet — and unlike the other cards, the sound usually arrives before the animal is ever seen.

    What does it mean?

    Listening for hidden birds is sound discrimination in the wild: locating a noise, matching it to a name. That hear-then-find chain is the foundation of all later listening skills.

    What does the child need to know?

    Birds vanish at the first shout, so the stealth trick is the lesson: hushed voices and slow feet are what bring birds closer. The stillness trick is a bonus skill for the grown-up too — patience, modelled out loud.

    Why this matters

    Birds are everywhere, every day, free of charge. This is the one animal card that keeps teaching after breakfast, after lunch and out of every window in town.

    What it teaches

    Listening and sound-locating, whisper-voice control, and the stillness habit — the first step of every nature watcher and every quiet game.

    Words to learn

    birdtweetlistenwingsquietsky

    Say this to your child

    “"Listen… tweet, tweet! A bird! Can you hear it? Whisper now — birds fly away from loud voices. Point at the bird. Tweet tweet — hello, bird!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say bird, then tweet tweet with a finger beak pecking the air.
    2. Take up position at a window or open door and hold a shared silence for a few slow seconds — count them in your head so you outlast the wiggle.
    3. When a bird sings or hops past, point and whisper "bird!" — whispering keeps the birds and makes the game exciting.
    4. When your toddler spots a bird before you do, hand over the win completely: "you found the bird! Tweet tweet!" Their find beats any card.
    5. Make the window listen a daily habit this week — breakfast, noon, dusk — and keep the card on the sill as the reminder.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a bird saying tweet. Find the bird, find the tweet, then ask where the bird’s wings are — wings are what make this card’s animal different from all the others.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the bird?" "What does the bird say?" "Can you hear a bird right now?" "Can you whisper like we do for birds?"

    What your child can say or do

    A pointing arm and a whispered "bir!" — the whisper is the triumph. Some toddlers freeze dramatically mid-step when a real bird lands; that freeze is the listening skill in action.

    Out in the real world

    Pigeons, gulls, sparrows and magpies are daily free lessons. Every street has birds; the game is simply remembering to stop and listen for the length of one slow breath.

    Try it together

    Bird-spotting walk: one street, five slow minutes, count the birds you find together on your fingers. One bird is a success. Point, whisper, move on — no chasing, ever.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the bird says. A tweet, a chirp or a pointing whisper passes. Then watch the window tomorrow — a toddler who stops and listens unprompted has taken the lesson outside.

    Parent tips

    Whisper is the whole atmosphere of this card, so keep your own voice low and the game lasts longer. A window-side card lives permanently after this week; birds never stop visiting.

    Staying safe

    We watch birds, we do not chase them — running at pigeons teaches the opposite of the game. Feeding is a grown-up job at the table, never from a toddler’s hand on the street.

    This lesson pairs with the Bird flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).
